articles.title: Lil Finder Guy pet was the gateway to building my own Mac apps with Codex
articles.subtitle: At the start of May, OpenAI released a playful feature inside its Codex desktop app for creating a virtual pet. This silly little addition solved my biggest challenge with Codex: what should I do with it?
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
At the start of May, OpenAI released a playful feature inside its Codex desktop app for creating a virtual pet.

This silly little addition solved my biggest challenge with Codex: what should I do with it? My first real task with Codex was putting together a virtual Lil Finder Guy for fun.

A month later, I’m using two Mac apps that Codex built at my direction. Toying around with Codex Pets was the gateway for me to better understand its capabilities.

OpenAI tools for making apps have improved a lot since last summer

Both Mac apps are just for my use and not intended for distribution, but that’s just a choice and not a Codex limitation. They’re genuinely usable and useful software applications that serve my needs.

One tool is called Flow, and it just helps me track activity and changes around the App Store. Another offers a better experience with using a social network on the Mac without certain constraints of Chrome, like minimum window width.

The experience taught me just how much these tools have changed since this time last year as well.

For example, I wanted to make my own Launchpad replacement when macOS Tahoe removed the feature from the Mac last June. (Launchpad wasn’t for everyone, but it was part of my muscle memory since OS X Lion. I’ve since moved on from missing it.)

Using ChatGPT to walk me through Xcode while copying and pasting blocks of code and screenshots of errors was a process void of much joy. Even as a proof-of-concept, I couldn’t get the app that I was making to resemble the behavior that I had in mind. Nuking the project felt good.

With Codex, I had a functioning app that solved my specific need in almost no time (and literally no Xcode). I was able to go from idea to minimum viable software almost immediately. The rest of my first month with Codex and making the app was spent adding features beyond my original need and getting more specific about how things should look and behave.

There are more tools that I want to make for myself next, and having Codex’s capabilities on the Mac has been a real boost.

(Next, I’ll be watching Apple’s WWDC announcements with a new eye for what additional capabilities become available. I’m also cautious about any changes that may break my newfound system for turning ideas into functioning tools.)

Computer Use in Codex is a major unlock

Part of what makes Codex good at this compared to my experience using ChatGPT a year ago is that the model and app are made for coding and generally just doing things for you.

ChatGPT will absorb most or all of this functionality as a feature within the main app, but the extent of this remains to be seen. For now, there’s one thing in particular about Codex that made all the difference in the world: Computer Use.

Codex is far from the only coding agent available on the Mac, and it’s not the only version with a computer use feature either. But Codex’s Computer Use feature is phenomenal. On the Mac, it works in the background without taking over your machine. For me, this has meant I’ve been able to use my Mac, uninterrupted, while this coding agent expertly follows my direction.

Codex’s Computer Use essentially unlocks the complete opposite experience from what ChatGPT provided in this department last summer. Instead of it providing me with guidance and not much perspective, I’ve been able to guide it and vastly expand my own perspective.

You don’t have to spend a lot to get Codex experience

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

Privacy is core

DC announced a new fighting game on Monday and — nope, calm down. It's not Injustice 3. I know you want Injustice 3. I too really want Injustice 3. This is not Injustice 3.

Instead, we're getting Dicko, a mobile game that's set to arrive in 2027. Wait, did I call it Dicko? Sorry, it's called DCKO, but you and I both know people are going to call it Dicko because people are already calling it Dicko.

DCKO is a 2v2 tag fighter with both online multiplayer PvP and single-player modes from developer Drop Fake. "It was important to us that DCKO represented a significant leap forward for the fighting game genre on mobile," creative director Gene Campbell said in a news release. "Live multiplayer games between players are core to the spirit of fighting games, and we are proud of the work we’ve done to bring this feature to mobile comic book fighters for the first time."

DCKO features plenty of DC heroes you know and a handful of B- and C-listers. You got your Batman, Superman, and Wonder Woman, of course. Zatanna, Constantine, Blue Beetle, and Katana are also joining the roster, which has 19 confirmed fighters at this time. You can check out the full roster at the game's website, and more characters will be revealed one at a time on a monthly basis.

DC K. O. was a similarly titled event that began in the pages of DC Comics last year. It put three dozen characters in a tournament with the universe on the line, and even featured crossover characters like The Boys' Homelander and Mortal Kombat's Sub-Zero. No one called DC K. O.

Dicko while the event was going on, which means DCKO probably should have borrowed the comic's space and periods to not look so much like "Dicko. " Despite essentially sharing a title, it doesn't seem like DCKO and DC K. O. are related in any way at this time.

You can preregister now for DCKO 's open beta. The full game will launch sometime in 2027 for iOS and Android.

articles.title: How to Swap Between Mac Window Layouts at the Touch of a Button With the Stream Deck and Moom
articles.subtitle: El Gato’s Stream Deck is a useful accessory that provides Mac users with extra buttons for assigning custom keystrokes, actions, launching apps and more.
articles.author: OWC Rocket Yard
articles.content:
El Gato’s Stream Deck is a useful accessory that provides Mac users with extra buttons for assigning custom keystrokes, actions, launching apps and more. Instead of memorizing a complex keyboard shortcut, for example, one could simply assign it to a button on the Stream Deck. Press the button, and the keyboard shortcut runs. Neat!

Up until now, I’ve been using my Stream Deck as a glorified control board for managing Zoom calls and launching a few specific applications. For Zoom calls, I’ve configured my Stream Deck’s buttons to quickly mute / unmute my microphone, increase / decrease my Mac’s speaker volume, and toggle my webcam on or off. It’s super convenient for those tasks.

But the Stream Deck is capable of so much more.

Could I use it with Moom?

As a refresher, Moom is a powerful window management tool for the Mac. For me, its chief strength is Moom’s ability to save custom window layouts. For example, when I’m writing articles for OWC’s Rocket Yard blog, I have a saved Moom window layout which includes BBEdit, Bloom, and a Safari window.

And when I’m recording videos for my YouTube channel, I have another Moom window layout which includes Recordly, Photoshop and KeyCastr. In total, I have 7 such window layouts within Moom that I switch between on a regular basis.

Prior to the Stream Deck, switching between my saved Moom layouts required a visit to the menu bar or remembering each layout’s assigned keyboard shortcut. Remembering the keyboard shortcut for each layout was difficult. And visiting my Mac mini’s already overcrowded menu bar introduced just enough friction to be a minor pain.

So I looked into solutions that would let me use my Stream Deck with Moom. And I found one. Before I spill the beans, let me share a list of the items you’ll need to pull such a feat.

El Gato Stream Deck 15-Key Control Panel ($149US)

Moom ($15US)

Moom Profile Activator Plugin for Stream Deck (free)

Key to this operation is the Moom Profile activator, which is freely available on GitHub. Download the plugin, right-click on the file and open it with El Gato’s Stream Deck software.

Next, select the Moom Profile plugin (which appears in Stream Deck’s “Custom” menu), and drag it over to one of your Stream Deck’s unused buttons. Finally, select the saved window layout (profile) that you want to assign to the button you’ve created. Your new buttons are automatically reflected on the Stream Deck hardware. To make the buttons easier to interpret at a glance, I’ve given each of them a custom icon, using Stream Deck’s software.

Being able to switch between each of my saved window layouts has given my productivity a tremendous boost. I no longer have to spend time rearranging my windows before starting any given task.

articles.title: Fallout 5: Here are 10 adjustments Bethesda should make for an improved experience
articles.subtitle: Make global cataclysms fun again. Recent months have been full of bad news for the games industry, but sometimes a little light shines through, like when Bethesda confirmed last week that Fallout 5 is in preproduction.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Make global cataclysms fun again.

Recent months have been full of bad news for the games industry, but sometimes a little light shines through, like when Bethesda confirmed last week that Fallout 5 is in preproduction. Since then, it’s been a little difficult to think about much else. We’re too busy imagining what the next installment in the series might look like, in a more perfect world. On that note, here are 10 things we want to see from Fallout 5, whenever it arrives.

1 A silent protagonist

Video games often feel like books or movies, and there’s no use in complaining about something so many people clearly love. Still, some games should follow design philosophies that prioritize letting players drop into the starring role. To self-insert, even. The Fallout games certainly are one such case.

And while Fallout 4 featured excellent voice work, we wouldn’t complain for one second if Bethesda were to leave speaking roles to the NPCs and companions the next time around. Let us pretend we are the ones wandering the wasteland, please, not watching from the audience or filming everything.

2 Set somewhere outside America

The Fallout games have famously explored various regions within a retro-futuristic, alternate history version of America in distress. And that has been fine, but there are other countries to consider. Entire continents, even. In the case of a nuclear war, they probably wouldn’t fare any better than North America. Their long histories and traditions would also provide interesting subject matter.

Imagine Paris or England, Germany or China. How about Egypt or Brazil? The possibilities aren’t endless, but they’re close enough, and Fallout hasn’t paid nearly enough attention to the rest of the world thus far.

3 A less derivative plot with broader themes

People suck, but in times of great turmoil, loss, and sacrifice, with humanity on the brink of extinction, it’s only natural to go right on being awful to one another rather than changing for the greater good. Sound familiar? Admittedly, actual nuclear calamity would put life in simpler terms than you or I can fully appreciate.

But that doesn’t mean fiction about it can’t explore the grim possibilities with a little more nuance. If you think about some of the great moments the medium has provided in the past, shades of gray have been key ingredients. Let’s see a little more of that from Fallout.

4 More diverse dialog options

Speaking of nuance, Fallout 4 ’s approach to dialogue could do with some spring cleaning. That game presented us with four responses to most dialog prompts. Two of those were versions of “yes” (one with added sarcasm), and two were versions of “no. ” What’s the point in going with four choices as the default if they don’t push the character exchanges in new directions?

When we pick one option over the other, it would also be nice to have a clearer idea about the different possible outcomes. The sarcasm shouldn’t go away, of course, but it would be nice to see conversations in Fallout 5 achieve more than they have in past entries.

5 Improved skill development

Traditional RPGs let their characters develop new skills over the course of an adventure, which Fallout presents as perks. Unlocking new perks in Fallout 4 was compelling in the extreme, allowing players to engage with the damaged world on their terms. However, there’s room for improvement.

If you blast a bunch of enemies and use that experience to level up your ability to speak eloquently, there’s a bit of a disconnect, don’t you think? The Elder Scrolls games already adopt a superior approach, in that the way you play the game impacts how you can develop your character.

Obsidian’s The Outer Worlds and its sequel also include flaws as a progression mechanic, which offset a negative trait with a positive one. (For instance, thieving players can trigger the Kleptomaniac flaw, which makes them automatically steal everything in their line of sight. It’s chaotic, but you can sell your ill-gotten goods to vendors for twice the usual price.
